name: Clean and dress a wound
summary: Irrigate the wound with the cleanest water you have, cover it, and watch it — infection is what kills days after the injury.
time: 10 minutes, then a look every day

materials.item: cordage or tape to hold the dressing

steps.text: Stop the bleeding first — see `bleeding-direct-pressure`. A wound that is still bleeding cannot be assessed.
Irrigate: flush the wound with a hard stream of clean water until visible dirt is gone. Volume and pressure do the work.
steps.why: Contamination left in a wound is the infection. Antiseptics poured on top of grit do very little.

steps.text: Leave deeply embedded objects where they are — bandage around them.
Cover with the cleanest dry material available and secure it without cutting off circulation.
Change the dressing daily, or whenever it is soaked or filthy, and look at the wound each time.

verify: Fingers or toes beyond the dressing stay warm, pink, and feel normal — otherwise it is too tight.
Daily check: spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, a red streak running toward the body, or a fever means infection is winning.
limits: Irrigation reduces the bacterial load. It does not sterilize a wound and it does not treat an infection that has already set in.
A wound that needs closing needs a clinician. Closing a contaminated wound in the field traps the infection inside.
No plant preparation in this corpus is a substitute for antibiotics in an established infection.
cautions: Do not pour strong antiseptics (undiluted iodine, hydrogen peroxide, alcohol) into open tissue — they kill the tissue trying to heal alongside the bacteria.
Animal and human bites, puncture wounds and anything from dirty water carry a high infection risk and are a reason to seek care rather than manage in place.
Tetanus is a real risk from any dirty wound.
